1086.title: Raga Jaitsri
1086.hook: Jaitsri opens with a hand placed on a forehead
1086.howItsDone: Shabads from the Jaitsri section of the Guru Granth Sahib are sung in Raga Jaitsri in kirtan, and Guru Ram Das's opening hymn, about the jewel of the Name and the Guru's hand on the forehead, is one of them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hymn in Dhanasri: aartis from the sky to a farmhouse kitchen. Your line: the sky's aarti. A new week starts.

Someone slips into a dark room at three in the morning, sits on the edge of a feverish child's bed, and lays a cool hand on the child's forehead. Nothing gets fixed. The fever is still there. But the room changes. That kind of strength doesn't shout. It arrives, it stays, and it steadies. Today's raga opens its pages with a hand like that. Today: Raga Jaitsri, which tradition links with longing and quiet strength.
screen: `A FEVER AT THREE IN THE MORNING.` → `A COOL HAND ON THE FOREHEAD.` → `STRENGTH THAT DOESN'T SHOUT.`

segments.voice: Jaitsri comes after Dhanasri in the Granth's order. Its first hymn is by Guru Ram Das, mahala four, and it begins with two pictures. In paraphrase: the jewel of the Name has come to dwell in my heart; the Guru has placed his hand on my forehead. The jewel is inside, hidden, precious, not for show. The hand is outside, a familiar gesture of blessing: an elder's palm resting on a younger head. A touch from outside, a treasure within. Now the longing. A raga of longing usually sounds like reaching for something far away. But this hymn starts from what has already been given. Its longing is to stay near the one who gave it, to keep feeling that hand. Strength and longing turn out to be one movement seen from two sides: you lean toward what steadies you. The hymn doesn't say the hard things vanished. It says something precious now lives inside, put there by a touch. Not the strength of a wall, which keeps everything out, but of a keel under a boat, unseen, keeping it upright in the wind. Jaitsri's opening pages are calm, and the calm has weight. Quiet strength.

segments.voice: If it feels right, rest your own palm lightly on your forehead for a few breaths and feel its weight and warmth, then let it fall to your lap and see whether the steadiness stays. Bring to mind someone whose presence has steadied you without a word, and stay with them a while, saying Waheguru softly if you pray, or simply remembering them if you don't.
Raga Jaitsri. The raga after Dhanasri, linked by tradition with longing and quiet strength, which opens with the jewel of the Name in the heart and the Guru's hand on the forehead. Today's word.
Your line: quiet strength. A keel under the boat, not a wall around it. See you tomorrow.

1087.title: A hymn in Jaitsri
1087.hook: Guru Arjan's Var in Jaitsri opens with a salok: whole at the beginning, the middle and the end
1087.howItsDone: Jaitsri ki Var is sung in kirtan with its saloks and pauris, and its opening salok, aad pooran madh pooran ant pooran, is sung and recited in gurdwaras and at home.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raga Jaitsri: the jewel in the heart and the Guru's hand on the forehead. Your line: quiet strength.

Beginning, middle, end. Somewhere in school, someone wrote those three words on a board and said every story has them. The beginning is full of promise. The middle sags; it's where people get lost, bored or stuck. The end, if it's a good one, ties things up. A lot of life happens in some middle or other. Near the end of the Jaitsri section, Guru Arjan begins a Var, a ballad, and its very first salok says something surprising about all three.
screen: `BEGINNING, MIDDLE, END.` → `THE MIDDLE SAGS.` → `A VAR BEGINS IN JAITSRI.`

segments.voice: A Var in the Granth is a ballad made of pauris, stanzas, with saloks, short verses, set before them, like small lamps carried ahead of each stanza. This one, Jaitsri ki Var, is Guru Arjan's, mahala five. Its opening salok begins: aad pooran, madh pooran, ant pooran, parmesurah. Aad: the beginning. Madh: the middle. Ant: the end. Pooran: full, whole, complete. In paraphrase: whole at the beginning, whole in the middle, whole at the end, is the Supreme Lord. Then: the saints remember the one who pervades everywhere, and Nanak calls that one the destroyer of wrongs, the Lord of the world. Look at the word in the middle. Madh pooran. Whole in the middle. That's where any story feels least whole: the middle of a long illness, of a degree, of grief, of an ordinary Wednesday. The salok doesn't say God is waiting at the end once you get through. It says the middle is just as full as the start and the finish. That's where this Var's strength comes from. Not a burst of courage for the big moment, but a fullness that doesn't thin out halfway, and the Var goes on, stanza by stanza, built on that first promise. Strength in jaitsri is the strength of the middle.

Then think of one thing in your life that's in its middle right now, unfinished, and let it be whole for the length of a breath, with Waheguru in each pause if you pray.

1088.title: Raga Todi
1088.hook: a morning raga that opens by admitting need
1088.howItsDone: Shabads from the Todi section of the Guru Granth Sahib are sung in Raga Todi in kirtan, including in morning programs at some gurdwaras, following the tradition that links Todi with the morning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hymn in Jaitsri: whole at the beginning, whole in the middle, whole at the end. Your line: strength in jaitsri.

The first minutes after waking are strange ones. The armor isn't on yet. Before the to-do list and the phone and the public face, there's a softer person blinking at the ceiling, who might, for a moment, say what they actually need. Tradition calls today's raga a morning raga, and a tender one. And the hymn that opens it sounds like that unguarded minute: no ceremony, no long praise, just an honest sentence about need. Today: Raga Todi.
screen: `THE FIRST MINUTES AFTER WAKING.` → `BEFORE THE ARMOR GOES ON.` → `AN HONEST SENTENCE ABOUT NEED.`

segments.voice: Todi comes after Jaitsri in the Granth's order. Its first hymn is by Guru Ram Das, mahala four. It begins: har bin reh na sakai man mera. In paraphrase: without the Lord, my mind cannot live. No argument, no description of God's greatness, just dependence, the way a child says I need you. That line opens the refrain, the rahao, the part the hymn keeps coming back to, and it goes on, in paraphrase: my beloved, the breath of my life, is the Lord; the Guru has brought me to meet him, and I won't be tossed again on the terrifying ocean of the world. Notice the order. First the need, said plainly. Then the beloved, named as breath, as close as the air going in and out. Then the meeting, and the steadiness that follows. That's what tender means here. Not weak, not sentimental. Tender is how a person sounds when they stop pretending to be self-sufficient. Tradition sets Todi in the morning, and teachers describe raga moods in different ways, so hold the hour lightly. But you can hear why these words would sit well at dawn, before the armor goes on. A tender morning.

Then quietly finish this sentence for yourself, without explaining it: without this, I couldn't live. A person, a faith, the breath itself; if you pray, the answer can be Waheguru.
Raga Todi. The short section after Jaitsri, a morning raga in tradition, which opens with Guru Ram Das saying: without the Lord, my mind cannot live. Today's word.

1089.title: Listening in Todi
1089.hook: a short Todi hymn that speaks to a mother: the Guru's feet are sweet
1089.howItsDone: Guru Arjan's Todi hymns, including maaee charan gur meethe, are sung in kirtan in Raga Todi, and Sikhs reading the Granth at home or in the sangat read them with their meanings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raga Todi, a morning raga that opens with a plain sentence of need. Your line: tender morning.

Maaee. Mother. A word called from the next room, or down the stairs, or into a phone. When something good happens, there can be one person you want to tell before anyone else: guess what, guess who I met. Today, slow right down and listen to one short hymn in Todi, word by word. It's by Guru Arjan, and it begins exactly like that: a voice turning to its mother to share something sweet. Today: listening in Todi.
screen: `MAAEE: MOTHER.` → `GUESS WHAT, GUESS WHO I MET.` → `ONE SHORT HYMN, LINE BY LINE.`

segments.voice: The heading says Todi, mahala five: Guru Arjan. Its refrain, the rahao, is the heart of it. Say the words slowly: maaee charan gur meethe. Maaee: mother, the way you'd call to her from the next room. Charan: feet. Gur: the Guru. Meethe: sweet. Mother, the Guru's feet are sweet. Feet may sound like an odd thing to call sweet. But in the Granth the Guru's feet are a picture of humility and closeness: you sit low, near the one you love, close enough to touch the dust they walk in. Calling them sweet is the language of affection, not of ceremony. The refrain goes on, in paraphrase: by great good fortune the Lord grants this, and the sight of the Guru brings fruit beyond counting. So it's shaped like a confidence: good news about the Guru, told to a mother, the way good news gets shared at a kitchen counter. Spoken to someone close, about someone loved, in the plainest speech there is: tender words. Yesterday's hymn said, without the Lord, my mind cannot live. Today's says, mother, it's sweet. Need, and then the sweetness of having it met.

segments.voice: Say the four words slowly, with a breath between each, maaee, charan, gur, meethe, or listen to a recording of this hymn with the words in front of you. Then sit in the quiet that follows and let someone come to mind you would run to with good news, living or gone, and stay with them, with Waheguru if you pray, or just letting them be close if you don't.

1090.title: Raga Bairari
1090.hook: a short raga whose first hymn tells the mind to listen to a story that can't be told
1090.howItsDone: Shabads from the short Bairari section of the Guru Granth Sahib are sung in Raga Bairari in kirtan, and because the section is brief, a reader can go through all of it in one sitting.

segments.voice: Yesterday, listening in Todi: maaee charan gur meethe, mother, the Guru's feet are sweet. Your line: tender words.

Small things can shine brightest in a room. A candle flame hides under a cupped hand, yet in the dark, eyes go straight to it. Some sections of the Guru Granth Sahib run on page after page. Today's isn't one of them. Raga Bairari is short enough to read in one sitting, and it comes right after Todi. But small doesn't mean dim. Its first hymn opens with a command to the mind and a subject bigger than any book. Today: Raga Bairari.
screen: `A CANDLE FLAME IS SMALL.` → `SHORT ENOUGH FOR ONE SITTING.` → `SMALL DOESN'T MEAN DIM.`

segments.voice: Bairari's hymns come from Guru Ram Das, mahala four, with Guru Arjan's voice there too. The first one opens: sun man, akath katha har naam. Sun: listen. Man: mind, the restless inner voice the Gurus speak to again and again. Akath: what can't be spoken. Katha: a story, a telling. Har naam: the Lord's Name. In paraphrase: listen, mind, to the untellable story of the Lord's Name. Stop on that phrase. Akath katha, an untellable telling: a story no one can finish saying, and yet the hymn asks you to listen to it. That's the brightness inside a small raga. The section is short, but what it points to has no edge. The hymn goes on, in paraphrase: through the Guru's teaching, meditate on the Lord, and peace and every kind of good will come. Notice that the first word isn't sing, or bow, or give. It's listen. The mind is told to stop talking and take something in. A short section is easy to hear whole, start to finish, and tomorrow that's exactly the plan. Small, because the pages are few. Bright, because of what they hold.

segments.voice: Say the hymn's first two words to yourself, sun man, listen, mind, and then do it: stop rehearsing and planning, and take in the sounds, the breath and the stillness under them. When the inner voice starts talking again, say sun man once more, gently, and go back to listening, with Waheguru as the one word you listen for, if you pray.
Raga Bairari. The short section after Todi, whose first hymn says sun man, listen, mind, to the untellable story of the Lord's Name. Today's word.
Your line: small and bright. Few pages, and no edge to what they hold. See you tomorrow.

1091.title: Listening in Bairari
1091.hook: a tiny raga, a few hymns, easy to hear whole
1091.howItsDone: Sikhs meet the Granth in daily shabads, in the hukamnama read at random each day, and in kirtan; some also read whole sections or the whole Granth through, and a short raga like Bairari can be read in one sitting.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raga Bairari, whose first hymn says sun man, listen, mind. Your line: small and bright.

The Guru Granth Sahib is easy to meet in pieces. One shabad in the morning. A hukamnama, the day's reading opened at random. A few lines sung in kirtan, then the next raga, the next Guru, the next page. A book this large invites that. Bairari offers something else: a whole section you can take in at once, start to finish, without losing the thread. A few hymns, a short stretch of pages, and then it's done. Today: listening in Bairari, all of it.
screen: `USUALLY IN PIECES.` → `ONE SHABAD, ONE HUKAMNAMA.` → `A WHOLE SECTION AT ONCE.`

segments.voice: It begins where yesterday left off, with Guru Ram Das: sun man, listen, mind, to the untellable story of the Lord's Name. More of his hymns follow, turning the same light around. One has a refrain worth carrying out of the room. It opens: har jan ram naam gun gaavai. In paraphrase: the Lord's servant sings the praises of the Name; and if anyone slanders that servant, the servant doesn't lose their own goodness. Slander is aimed at someone, but here it can't take anything from them. The goodness stays where it was. Then the voice changes. Guru Arjan, mahala five, closes the section, and his hymn moves from the single listener to a crowd: in paraphrase, the saints met together and sang the Lord's praise, and the pains of countless lifetimes went away. Hear the whole arc. A mind told to listen. A servant who can't be robbed of goodness by someone else's words. A gathering, singing together. Alone, then under pressure, then a sangat. Read one hymn and you get a line. Read all of Bairari and you get a little journey, from listening alone to singing together: the whole of it.
screen: `FIRST: LISTEN, MIND.` · `SLANDER CAN'T TAKE THE GOODNESS.` · `GURU ARJAN: THE SAINTS SING TOGETHER.` · `ALONE, UNDER PRESSURE, TOGETHER.` · then, large: `THE WHOLE OF IT.`

segments.voice: If you have a Gurbani app or a printed Granth with meanings, read the Bairari pages straight through, slowly, or play its shabads one after another. Then sit and hold the shape of it, listening, steadiness, singing together, the way you'd hold a short letter after reading it, without picking a favorite line; if you pray, say Waheguru at the end.
Listening in Bairari. The short raga heard whole: a mind told to listen, a servant slander can't rob, and the saints singing together. Today's word.
Your line: the whole of it. Tomorrow, Raga Tilang, where the colors change again. Go gently.

1092.title: Raga Tilang
1092.hook: a raga with Persian color, where Guru Nanak speaks in words his Muslim neighbors used
1092.howItsDone: In kirtan, ragis sing shabads from the Tilang section of the Guru Granth Sahib in Raga Tilang, and listeners can hear in Guru Nanak's opening hymn the Persian and Arabic names for God, such as Karim and Parvardigar.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bairari, small enough to hear from start to finish. Your line: the whole of it. This week ends today: Jaitsri's quiet strength, Todi's tender morning, Bairari, and now Tilang.

Yak araj guftam pes tu. Those are the first words under the heading Raga Tilang, on ang seven twenty-one of the Guru Granth Sahib. Say them aloud and they don't sound like the Punjabi of the hymns before them. The words lean toward Persian, and a few lines later come names for God that Muslim neighbors in Guru Nanak's Punjab used. Same Guru, same book, same message, in a different set of clothes. Today: Raga Tilang, and why a song might change its accent.
screen: `YAK ARAJ GUFTAM PES TU.` → `A DIFFERENT ACCENT.` → `SAME GURU, SAME BOOK.`

segments.voice: Tilang follows little Bairari, and its section opens with Guru Nanak. First, the plea, in plain English: I have made one petition before you; lend it your ear, Creator. Then the praise: you are true, great, generous, without flaw, the Sustainer. Then a hard turn. The world is a place you pass through; know it for certain, heart. The angel of death has me by the hair, and the heart hasn't understood. Second, the color. Listen to the names inside that praise: Karim, the generous one. Parvardigar, the one who sustains. Azrael, the angel of death. These are Persian and Arabic words that Muslims in Punjab used. Some readers hear Tilang as a place where Guru Nanak speaks to Muslim listeners in their own words. He doesn't argue with their vocabulary. He prays in it. The one God of the Granth's opening lines is still the one addressed; only the accent has changed, the way a good host greets a guest in the guest's language. That's the persian color. Third, the ending, which needs no translation. Nanak says: your servant is the dust under the feet of your servants. A petition that started by asking to be heard ends by asking to be low.
screen: `TILANG FOLLOWS LITTLE BAIRARI.` · `ONE PLEA: LEND YOUR EAR, CREATOR.` · `KARIM, PARVARDIGAR: PERSIAN COLOR.` · `THE DUST UNDER YOUR SERVANTS' FEET.` · then, large: `PERSIAN COLOR.`

segments.voice: If you'd like, play a shabad in Raga Tilang, or bring to mind one person whose words for the deepest things differ from yours: a neighbor, a coworker, a grandparent. Don't translate them; just hear them the way they'd say it, and let those words be welcome beside your breath, with one soft Waheguru if you pray.
Raga Tilang. The raga after Bairari, where Guru Nanak's opening plea leans toward Persian and calls God Karim and Parvardigar. Today's word.
Your line: persian color. Not a different faith, a different set of words reaching for the same One. A week done.
